title: Early-life hallmarks of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity
authors: Tsang, R. S. M.; Stow, D.; Katzourou, I. K.; LINC Consortium, ; van den Bree, M. B. M.; Khandaker, G. M.; Timpson, N. J.
abstract: BackgroundInternalizing disorders and cardiometabolic disease are common conditions that frequently co-occur in later life and may be attributed to shared genetic influences. While phenotypic effects of polygenic liability of adult disorders may emerge early in life, studies have not investigated this in the context of multimorbidity. This study set out to investigate early manifestations of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity (ICM-MM) in a UK population birth cohort. MethodsWe used data from 5,934 individuals in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC). We modelled trajectories of 12 mental and cardiometabolic health outcomes using mixed effects models, and investigated effects of adult ICM-MM polygenic liability on these trajectories. We also investigated associations of adult ICM-MM polygenic liability with circulating inflammatory proteins (Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel) at ages 9 and 24. ResultsAdult ICM-MM polygenic liability is associated with cardiometabolic traits and inflammation, and with changes in depressive symptoms and cardiometabolic traits over time in childhood through to early adulthood. A notable early life biological footprint is inflammation. We found that higher ICM-MM polygenic liability is consistently associated with higher interleukin-6 (IL6), tumor necrosis family superfamily member 14 (TNFSF14) and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) levels in both childhood and early adulthood. ConclusionsAdult ICM-MM polygenic liability manifests early in life through changes in mental and cardiometabolic health and blood biomarkers, especially in increases of circulating inflammatory proteins related to obesity, immune cell chemotaxis and migration that may contribute to disease pathogenesis by seeding inflammation in relevant tissues.

infographic.key_insight: Genetic liability to adult internalizing–cardiometabolic multimorbidity is associated with early-life mental and cardiometabolic changes and higher levels of inflammatory proteins.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings highlight potential early biological pathways linking mental and cardiometabolic conditions, but do not establish clinical screening or treatment strategies.
method: Studied 5,934 participants in the UK ALSPAC birth cohort.
Used mixed-effects models to assess associations between polygenic liability and trajectories of 12 health outcomes.
Examined circulating inflammatory proteins at ages 9 and 24 using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel.
infographic.evidence_signal: Higher polygenic liability was consistently associated with higher IL6, TNFSF14 and HGF levels at both ages 9 and 24.
infographic.watch_item: Observational associations in one UK cohort do not establish causality or generalizability; this is not an AI cancer drug discovery study.
infographic.paper_title: Early-life hallmarks of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity

title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
authors: Fathi Kazerooni, A.; Batal, F.; Vunnava, B.; Damaraju, E.; Tavallaii, A.; Gandhi, D.; Gottipati, A.; Zhu, P.; Chrysochoou, D.; Varshochi, S.; Adib Moradi, S.; Familiar, A. M.; Chiang, A.; Vaghani, Y.; Azemi, G.; Doig, M.; To, M.-S.; Luck, A.; Kim, M. C.; Khalili, N.; Khalili, N.; Jain, P.; Lee, C.; Hansford, J. R.; Di Ieva, A.; Storm, P. B.; Resnick, A. C.; Reddy, K.; Vossough, A.; Nabavizadeh, A.
abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

infographic.key_insight: PedDx classifies pediatric posterior fossa tumors from MRI, with higher accuracy among cases retained after confidence-based abstention.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This diagnostic AI research—not drug discovery—may inform future imaging-based assessment, but does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Segmentation-free analysis of T2-weighted MRI using pretrained 3DINO representations.
Agentic workflow producing predictions and structured quality-control reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external-validation and 40 independently tested cases; accuracy was 79.8%, 81.4% and 92.5% in the three test cohorts, rising to 90.5%, 88.7% and 97.3% among non-abstained cases.
infographic.watch_item: Out-of-distribution testing revealed confidently incorrect predictions, while imaging perturbations exposed acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities.
infographic.paper_title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation

title: Sex and Gender Reporting and Female Participation Relative to Disease Burden in ClinicalTrials.gov
authors: Green, M. D.; Aziz, M.; Sullenger, R. D.; Yoo, B. J.; O'Brien, E. C.; Navar, A. M.; Duroseau, B.; Thorpe, R. J.; Brantner, C. L.
abstract: ImportanceAssessing representation by sex assigned at birth and gender identity requires reporting of both in trials. If disclosure of full gender and sex participation from clinicaltrials.gov this is limited, it poses challenges in characterization and understanding of those participant experiences. ObjectiveTo determine how often ClinicalTrials.gov trials published trials report sex and gender, which characteristics are associated with reporting, and how participants female share compares with that of the general public. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsCross-sectional study of interventional trials registered to ClinicalTrials.gov, with or without US sites, with primary completion on or after September 27, 2008, and results first posted from January 1, 2009, through April 30, 2026. ExposuresFunder type, phase, US sites, enrollment, primary completion year, number of countries, and therapeutic area. Main Outcomes and MeasuresReporting of sex and gender, and the female participation-to-prevalence ratio (PPR; trial female share divided by the number of people with the condition). ResultsAmong 58,007 trials (median enrollment, 72 [IQR, 31 to 206]; 42,644 [74%] with US sites), 553 (0.95%) reported gender and 57,683 (99.44%) reported sex. Gender reporting was more common with National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding (odds ratio [OR], 9.05; 95% CI, 6.65 to 12.6), US sites (OR, 4.21; 95% CI, 2.96 to 6.22), and larger enrollment. Across 10 conditions (15,552 mixed-sex trials), median PPR ranged from 0.68 (95% CI, 0.64 to 0.71) for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to 1.05 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.09) for obesity and had a relatively lower female share in 8. Among the 10 conditions most prevalent in our cohort, 6,917 of 16,097 trial condition combinations (43.0%) reached a PPR of at least 0.90; odds of reaching it were higher for NIH-funded (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11 to 1.34) and lower for government-funded trials (OR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.33) as compared to industry-funded trials. Conclusions and RelevanceIn ClinicalTrials.gov, sex reporting is nearly universal, whereas gender reporting is concentrated among NIH-funded, US-based, and larger trials. Female trial enrollment fell below the female share of people with the condition for most conditions, emphasizing the benefit of condition-specific benchmarks in clinical trials.

infographic.key_insight: Across ClinicalTrials.gov trials, sex reporting was nearly universal, gender reporting was rare, and female participation was generally low relative to disease burden.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Incomplete gender reporting and female underrepresentation can limit assessment of how broadly trial findings apply.
method: Cross-sectional analysis of 58,007 interventional trials with posted results.
Assessed reporting associations with funding, location, enrollment, and other trial characteristics.
Compared female trial participation with female disease prevalence using participation-to-prevalence ratios (PPRs) across 10 conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Sex was reported in 99.44% of trials and gender in 0.95%; 43.0% of 16,097 trial–condition combinations achieved a female PPR of at least 0.90.
infographic.watch_item: This observational registry analysis identifies reporting and representation gaps, not their causes; it does not evaluate AI or cancer drug discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Sex and Gender Reporting and Female Participation Relative to Disease Burden in ClinicalTrials.gov

title: Deep Time-to-Event Models for Intrapartum Fetal Monitoring
authors: Imai Aldeia, G. S.; Coggan, H.; Yang, Y.; Levine, L.; McCoy, J. A.; La Cava, W.
abstract: Timely detection of fetal distress during labor is a central pursuit of modern obstetric care. The primary measure used in this regard is fetal heart rate and contraction monitoring (echocar-diotocography or CTG), which provides a continuous signal during labor. The vast majority of machine learning applications to CTG assume access to a 30 to 60 minute window just prior to delivery, which makes an untenable assumption that the timing of delivery is known. In this work, we reframe the problem as a time-to-event prediction task. We develop deep time-to-event models to predict the joint probability of imminent delivery and fetal acidosis, a biomarker of fetal hypoxia collected from umbilical cord gas after delivery. We develop a framework for this problem, drawing on deep discrete-time survival methods and marked point processes, adapting each to this particular setting (i.e., continuous physiological signals, fully observed events, partially observed labels). One approach dubbed Marked DeepHit accurately estimates acidemic delivery within one hour at multiple elapsed-time land-marks, with test-set AUROC of 0.837 [95% CI 0.692-0.970] and 0.935 [0.858-0.964] at 6 and 12 hours into labor, respectively. We find that these models also achieve competitive performance near delivery time compared to prior models trained specifically on the end of tracing, and outperform other clinical feature-based proposals, both on internal and external validation at a second site. These results give a proof-of-principle to support prospective evaluation of AI-EFM during labor. Data and Code AvailabilityWe use data from a multi-site academic health system (University of Pennsylvania Health System) and the CTU-UHB repository (Chuda[c]ek et al., 2014). Access to CTU-UHB is openly available under the terms of the data use agreement on Physionet. Code for this paper is available at https://github.com/cavalab/deep-tte-intrapartum-fetal-monitoring. Institutional Review Board (IRB)This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at University of Pennsylvania under a waiver of informed consent.

infographic.key_insight: Marked DeepHit predicts the joint probability of imminent delivery and fetal acidosis from labor-monitoring signals without assuming delivery timing is known.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This fetal-monitoring research—not cancer drug discovery—could support earlier recognition of acidemic delivery risk, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Reframes continuous fetal heart rate and contraction monitoring as time-to-event prediction.
Adapts deep discrete-time survival models and marked point processes.
Models delivery timing and partially observed fetal acidosis labels jointly.
infographic.evidence_signal: Test-set AUROC for acidemic delivery within one hour was 0.837 (95% CI 0.692–0.970) at 6 hours into labor and 0.935 (0.858–0.964) at 12 hours; evaluations also included external validation at a second site.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective evaluation is needed to establish real-time reliability and clinical usefulness before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Time-to-Event Models for Intrapartum Fetal Monitoring

title: MorphoStain: Physics-Guided Latent Diffusion and Morphological Distillation for Multiplex Stain Decomposition in Alzheimer's Neuropathology
authors: Saraei, M.; Zand, M.; Rahmani, S.
abstract: Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) enables simultaneous biomarker profiling, yet unmixing colocalized targets with identical spectra, such as dual-DAB marking Tau and Amyloid-{beta} in Alzheimers pathology, remains mathematically ill-posed. We propose MorphoStain, an unsupervised, physics-guided framework for morphological stain decomposition with epistemic uncertainty quantification. MorphoStain models stain separation via a conditional Latent Diffusion Teacher operating on a Beer- Lambert optical-density manifold, guided by pathology foundation models. To enable real-time clinical throughput, the teacher is distilled into a FastStudentU-Net (0.12M parameters, > 1,400 x compression), while a Symmetric Morphological Routing Module dynamically disentangles identical chromogen overlap. Evaluated on 9,908 held-out patches from the SEA-AD cohort, MorphoStain achieves 40.56 dB PSNR and 0.9961 SSIM at 140.1 FPS, showing statistically significant gains over InverseAE (Cohens d = 3.52) and NMF (Cohens d = 7.02), with p < 0.001 for both comparisons.

infographic.key_insight: MorphoStain uses physics-guided AI to separate overlapping Tau and amyloid-β staining in Alzheimer’s neuropathology, not cancer drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support neuropathology biomarker analysis, but the abstract does not establish diagnostic utility or clinical readiness.
method: Unsupervised latent diffusion models stain separation on a Beer–Lambert optical-density manifold.
Morphological routing disentangles targets sharing the same chromogen.
Teacher distillation produces a compact 0.12-million-parameter U-Net with uncertainty quantification.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 9,908 held-out SEA-AD patches, the authors report 40.56 dB PSNR, 0.9961 SSIM and 140.1 FPS, with significant gains over InverseAE and NMF (both p < 0.001).
infographic.watch_item: Identical-spectrum separation is inherently ill-posed; external-cohort validation and confirmation of biological fidelity remain important.
infographic.paper_title: MorphoStain: Physics-Guided Latent Diffusion and Morphological Distillation for Multiplex Stain Decomposition in Alzheimer's Neuropathology
